title: Three.js Newton's cradle: Opus vs Astra 6
author: ivanainai
prompt:
Build a complete, single-file HTML/Three.js experience showing an exceptionally beautiful, interactive Newton’s cradle.

Use the attached image as the reference for the recognizable construction: five polished metal balls suspended inside two parallel chrome frames.

The result should feel like a luxury product filmed in a real photography studio, with convincing materials, graceful pendulum motion, and working collision physics.

Open directly into the finished scene. The first rendered frame must already be composed beautifully enough to use as a video thumbnail.

Prioritize three things equally: the beauty of the chrome, the physical construction, and the correctness of the motion.

Create a square, recording-ready composition that adapts to the browser without stretching. Center one substantial Newton’s cradle on a seamless warm-ivory studio surface.

Use a fixed camera positioned mostly in front of the cradle, slightly above the balls and slightly off-center. Show enough depth to distinguish the front and rear frames, while keeping all five balls easy to count.

Use a restrained product-photography perspective, approximately equivalent to a 70mm lens. Avoid a wide-angle appearance.

The cradle should fill most of the image. Leave comfortable margins for the full outward swing on both sides. Neither the balls nor the frame may leave the image during normal operation.

Keep the camera stationary throughout. No orbiting, automatic zoom, camera shake, or cuts.

Construct exactly five identical, perfectly round polished stainless-steel spheres.

At rest, their centers must form one horizontal row, with neighboring spheres touching. Their diameters, masses, and suspension lengths must match.

Use two slender, parallel, inverted-U chrome support frames with rounded corners, positioned in front of and behind the ball row.

Each ball must hang from two fine, taut suspension wires: one connected to the front support and one to the rear support. These wires constrain its motion to the shared vertical swing plane.

Include small, believable attachment details. The wires must connect visibly to the balls and frame.

The support frame and anchors remain completely stationary. Update the suspension geometry from the actual ball positions every frame. Wires must never stretch, disconnect, pass through the spheres, or wave independently.

Choose elegant proportions: substantial spheres, slender tubular supports, and enough suspension length for a satisfying swing. Avoid thick ropes, oversized frames, and a bulky decorative base.

Make the metal look convincingly reflective.

Use physically based metallic materials, high-quality sphere geometry, restrained surface roughness, and a carefully designed reflection environment.

Create large studio-softbox reflections that wrap naturally around the spheres and curved frame. Include broad bright highlights, darker reflected regions, and subtle warm tones from the studio.

The spheres must retain readable volume. Avoid flat gray metal, featureless white balls, plastic shading, and excessive bloom.

Build the reflection environment procedurally inside the file. Do not depend on downloaded HDR images or external texture assets.

Use a large soft key light from the upper-left, gentle fill from the opposite side, and a restrained rim light to define the metal against the background.

Add soft contact shadows beneath the frame and moving shadows beneath the balls. Shadows should follow the motion and help communicate height.

Keep the background uncluttered, with a very subtle ivory gradient. The overall image should feel calm, precise, and expensive.

Implement a working simplified Newton’s cradle simulation.

Represent each sphere as an equal-mass pendulum with an angular position and angular velocity. Gravity must drive the swing. Derive the sphere positions from the pendulum geometry.

Use stable time integration and collision handling that can propagate impacts through the full chain of touching balls.

A fixed timestep with sufficient substeps, event-based impacts, or a suitable constraint-aware solver is acceptable. Choose an approach that remains stable at different rendering frame rates.

Do not animate the balls with unrelated sine waves or a prerecorded sequence. The motion must respond to the simulated state and user input.

The required behavior is:

Release one outer ball. It swings into the row, transfers its motion through the chain, and approximately one ball swings outward at the opposite end.
The outgoing ball returns, strikes the row, and sends the original outer ball outward again.
Release two adjacent balls together from one side. Approximately two balls must swing outward together from the opposite side.
The remaining balls should stay close to their resting positions, allowing small physically plausible movement during impacts.
Motion transfers at contact. The outgoing balls must not begin swinging before the incoming balls reach the row.

Handle the chain of contacts consistently. A single order-dependent collision pass must not produce a different result when the direction reverses.

Collisions should approximately conserve momentum and kinetic energy over the brief impact interval, with small losses. Use gentle damping so the swing amplitude decreases gradually.

The simulation must not gain energy, accelerate indefinitely, visibly interpenetrate, jitter continuously, or send the entire row swinging after every impact.

The balls should accelerate toward the bottom of their arcs and slow naturally near their turning points. Avoid constant-speed swinging.

Start with the leftmost ball raised approximately 35 degrees and the other four hanging at rest. Hold this initial pose briefly, around 0.4 seconds, then release automatically.

The experience must immediately demonstrate the classic alternating motion without requiring a click. Continue running without an automatic reset.

Add a small, elegant control strip near the bottom edge with:

“1 BALL”
“2 BALLS”
Pause / Resume
Reset
“0.25×” slow motion

Keep these controls visually secondary. They must not overlap the cradle or its swing paths.

Selecting “1 BALL” or “2 BALLS” should reset the simulation, raise the corresponding leftmost ball or pair to the same release angle, briefly hold, and release.

Reset should restore and replay the currently selected mode.

Slow motion must scale simulated time while preserving the same physics. It must not change gravity, collision behavior, or suspension geometry.

Allow the user to drag either outer ball outward within its permitted swing plane, then release it. Clamp the drag angle to a sensible maximum, around 45 degrees. Keep its suspension wires taut throughout.

Add an “H” keyboard shortcut to hide or reveal the controls for clean recording.

Keep the experience silent. No music, collision sounds, particles, motion trails, impact flashes, explanatory overlays, large titles, model names, or decorative text.

Deliver one complete HTML file with inline CSS and JavaScript. Use one consistently pinned Three.js version and matching modules if needed.

No build step, backend, external models, external textures, or HDR downloads.

Initialize the renderer, camera, lighting, materials, and starting pose before revealing the canvas. Avoid a visible black startup frame.

Support browser resizing without distorting the scene. Aim for smooth performance on a normal laptop and cap pixel density sensibly.

Before finishing, check that:

Exactly five spheres remain visible and correctly suspended.
The complete frame and maximum swing fit inside the square composition.
One-ball mode transfers approximately one ball at each impact.
Two-ball mode transfers approximately two balls at each impact.
Pause, reset, slow motion, and dragging work.
Chrome reflections remain readable throughout the motion.
The scene appears immediately and produces no runtime errors.

Return the complete working HTML.

title: 'The First Spark' procedural hand-drawn short
author: morpheusdv
prompt:
PROJECT: THE FIRST SPARK — Procedural Animated Short Film

You are a senior creative coder, generative artist, animation director, and JavaScript graphics engineer.

Your task is to create a visually stunning, fully animated short film using procedural JavaScript drawing.

I have attached a reference image showing a minimalist black-ink animation on an off-white background.

Use the reference to understand the visual language, but create an original animation with its own story, composition, and movement.

Do not create a slideshow, static illustration, or simple particle demo. Build a genuine animated short film with evolving scenes, expressive character animation, cinematic transitions, and continuous visual storytelling.

1. Technical requirements

Build the project using:

JavaScript
HTML5 Canvas 2D
requestAnimationFrame for real-time playback
Procedural geometry and vector-based drawing
Bezier curves, paths, particles, and custom brush strokes
Deterministic animation based on a master timeline

All visual elements must be generated through JavaScript code.

Do not use:

AI image-generation APIs
AI video-generation APIs
External images or pre-rendered video
Stock footage
CSS-only animation
Static illustrations disguised as animation

The animation must be genuinely generated by code.

You may use lightweight JavaScript libraries if they meaningfully improve the animation, but prioritize Canvas 2D.

2. Visual direction

Create a hand-drawn, minimalist, experimental animation.

Visual characteristics:

Warm off-white paper background
Deep black ink illustrations
Slightly imperfect hand-drawn outlines
Organic brush strokes
Variable line thickness
Ink splashes and subtle paper grain
Expressive silhouette-based character design
Fluid, organic movement
Occasional dramatic camera movements
Cinematic composition

The visual result should feel like a professional independent animated short film.

Avoid generic geometric motion graphics, repetitive particle effects, and simple bouncing shapes.

Every scene should have a clear visual purpose.

3. Story: THE FIRST SPARK

Create an original 60-second animated short film.

The story follows a tiny character that emerges from a drop of black ink and gradually discovers how to create a world.

SCENE 1 — THE BEGINNING (0–8 seconds)

An empty off-white canvas.

A tiny black ink droplet appears in the center.

The droplet begins trembling.

Small irregular brush strokes emerge from it.

The ink slowly transforms into a tiny living character.

The character opens its eyes and looks around.

The camera gradually moves closer.

SCENE 2 — DISCOVERY (8–18 seconds)

The character begins walking across the empty world.

Its movement must feel alive, with animated limbs, body deformation, and subtle secondary motion.

Every step leaves behind small ink marks.

The character notices one of these marks and touches it.

The mark begins growing into an organic structure.

SCENE 3 — CREATION (18–32 seconds)

The character discovers that its movements can create new objects.

It draws a line through the air.

The line becomes a tree.

More brush strokes emerge and transform into hills, plants, and abstract structures.

The camera follows the character as the world expands.

Objects must visibly grow and transform through procedural drawing rather than suddenly appearing.

SCENE 4 — CHAOS (32–44 seconds)

The character loses control of its creation.

Black ink spreads rapidly.

The landscape becomes distorted.

Trees twist into abstract shapes.

Ink splashes fill the screen.

The camera shakes subtly as the character runs.

The animation becomes faster and more intense.

Use fluid transitions between all visual elements.

SCENE 5 — THE FIRST SPARK (44–55 seconds)

The character stops running.

Everything becomes still.

A small glowing point appears in its hand.

This is the only moment where a subtle warm accent color may be used.

The character releases the light.

The light expands into a circular wave.

The chaotic ink reorganizes into a beautiful, balanced landscape.

The camera pulls back to reveal the completed world.

SCENE 6 — ENDING (55–60 seconds)

The character stands on a small hill and looks toward the horizon.

The camera slowly moves backward.

The entire landscape gradually transforms into a single small ink drawing on the original empty canvas.

Fade to off-white.

End.

4. Animation quality requirements

This is the most important part of the project.

Every scene must contain actual animation.

The character must have:

Procedurally animated walking and running
Expressive body language
Head and body rotation
Squash and stretch
Anticipation and follow-through
Smooth transitions between poses

Environmental elements must have:

Organic growth animations
Continuous subtle movement
Non-repetitive procedural variation
Smooth transformations between shapes

Implement a virtual camera with:

Position
Zoom
Rotation
Smooth tracking
Cinematic easing

Use layered depth and camera movement to create visual richness.

Do not rely on random movement alone.

The animation should be deliberately choreographed around the story.

5. Timeline and rendering architecture

Create a centralized animation timeline.

Every visual state must be determined by the current timeline position.

Implement a function similar to:

renderFrame(time)

The function must render the correct animation frame for any requested timestamp.

Use seeded randomness so that rendering the same timestamp always produces the same image.

Do not make the animation dependent on the number of previous frames rendered.

This is essential for deterministic video export.

Target specifications:

Resolution: 1920 × 1080

Aspect ratio: 16:9

Frame rate: 30 FPS

Duration: 60 seconds

Provide an option to switch to 1080 × 1920 vertical format for social media.

6. Preview and controls

Create a local web interface that allows me to:

Play and pause the animation
Restart the animation
Scrub through the timeline
Jump between scenes
Adjust playback speed
Switch between horizontal and vertical formats
Preview the animation in real time

Display the current timestamp and scene name.

7. Video export

Implement a reliable video export workflow.

The final animation must be exportable as a high-quality MP4 file.

Use deterministic frame-by-frame rendering to avoid dropped frames or inconsistent timing.

You may use a suitable browser rendering pipeline, a frame-sequence exporter, or FFmpeg.

Do not assume that recording the browser window in real time is sufficient for production-quality export.

Provide a simple export command or interface.

8. Development process

Do not attempt to create the entire film as one enormous, untested code block.

Work in stages.

First:

Create the project architecture.
Implement the Canvas rendering engine.
Implement the deterministic timeline.
Create the character animation system.
Build Scene 1 as a fully functional visual prototype.
Run the project and inspect the visual result.

After the first scene works, continue implementing the remaining scenes.

Test the animation at multiple timestamps.

Check for rendering errors, broken transitions, inconsistent character proportions, and performance problems.

If a scene looks too simplistic, improve its procedural drawing and choreography.

9. Deliverables

Provide:

Complete JavaScript source code
Working local animation preview
Editable scene definitions
Reusable character animation system
Reusable procedural drawing functions
Video export functionality
Instructions for running the project

The final result must be a functioning animation, not just a technical demonstration.

Start by implementing the first scene and the core animation engine. Once the prototype is functional, continue with the remaining scenes.

title: Red panda Koda and the giant peach
author: HeyAbhishek
prompt:
Create an exactly 30-second vertical 9:16 premium 3D animated adventure-comedy short. Use the attached @ Koda character sheet as the exact visual reference for Koda. Maintain his identical face, amber-brown eyes, cream facial markings, rust-red fur, dark legs, rounded ears, compact proportions and enormous ringed fluffy tail throughout every frame. The reference defines Koda's appearance only.
The entire story takes place on one continuous sunny green mountain hillside surrounded by distant forested mountains. One old peach tree grows from the slope. It has a thick stable trunk, several strong main branches and one thinner flexible outer branch. One enormous ripe golden-orange peach hangs near the end of that thinner branch. A large dense leafy bush grows directly below that side of the tree. A long fallen bamboo pole lies several meters away on the same hillside. Farther downhill, a narrow wooden footbridge crosses a shallow mountain stream. Keep this geography fixed throughout the entire video.
Koda desperately wants the enormous peach. His first idea is simply to climb the tree. He reaches the fruit but moves too far onto the thin outer branch, causing the branch to bend gradually under his weight. He almost touches the peach, loses traction and slides off into the huge soft bush below. Koda refuses to give up. He returns with the long fallen bamboo pole, places it diagonally against a strong fork in the tree and climbs it like a simple ladder. This time he reaches the peach and pulls it free. The peach is far heavier than expected, drops onto the clearly sloping hillside and begins rolling downhill because of gravity. Koda chases it, jumps onto the rolling fruit and accidentally begins riding it. He becomes thrilled and celebrates until he notices a narrow wooden footbridge directly ahead. The peach is much wider than the bridge entrance. title: Interactive 3D jelly orange in browser
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Whole Orange Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (inline JS/CSS, no libraries): a real-time WebGPU soft-body whole orange made of jelly. The user can grab and stretch it, and cut it with a knife into wheels, wedges and small pieces. Every piece is its own wobbling body.

Shape and pieces
- The orange is a signed distance field: a gently oblate ellipsoid (polar half-length 1.27 along x, equatorial radius 1.36) lying on its side, with a softly flattened seat on the floor.
- Every piece is that field clipped by the half-spaces n·X ≤ c of the cuts that made it, with the fresh edges rounded (smooth max, k ≈ 0.085). All pieces share the orange's original rest frame, so the anatomy stays where it grew.
- Per piece:
- a surface-nets render skin (0.042 grid) projected onto the field;
- a hex lattice for the simulation in the piece's own principal frame, with boundary nodes snapped to the surface;
- barycentric embedding of render vertices into the lattice tets.
- Up to 30 pieces; slivers are rejected.

Anatomy (all in rest space, so every cut shows it where it really is)
- Zest (0.07 deep) with oil-gland pores, a mottled tone, a green stem button at one end and a small navel at the other.
- White pith (to 0.19 deep).
- 11 segments around the stem axis, with thin milky membrane walls (slightly jittered, bowed and wandering along the axis) and a pithy core along the axis.
- Juice vesicles: teardrop sacs fanning out from the core within each segment.
- 16 pale citrus pips near the core, pointed end inward; a few small bubbles in the flesh.
- A pip that a cut goes through is kept by the side holding its centre and eased just under the new face.

Physics (XPBD)
- Per piece: hex cells with co-rotational shape matching plus volume constraints on their five tets.
- Zest and pith firmer than the flesh.
- Edge and deformation damping; floor contact with Coulomb friction and a little rolling resistance.
- Piece–piece contact against each other's exact rest shape in a best-fit frame.
- Sleeping pieces that wake on touch; fixed 60 Hz step with small substeps.

Knife
- A nakiri-style knife: draw a stroke across the orange.
- The stroke, read on the top of what it crosses, fixes a vertical blade plane, carried into each crossed piece's rest frame by its best-fit rotation and added as a half-space.
- The new pieces are built incrementally while the knife lines up, presses a groove and cuts straight down. They take over the position and speed of the jelly they came from, and the blade wedges the faces apart.

Rendering (WebGPU / WGSL)
- Procedural photo studio. Soft PCSS key shadow tinted by the jelly, plus contact AO from a height map.
- Back-face thickness; refraction of the scene, with each tap dimmed by its own path length.
- A volumetric march through the jelly in rest space, using a per-vertex inverse deformation gradient:
- zest, pith, membranes/core and flesh each absorb with their own colour (Beer–Lambert);
- scattering is grey (only absorption is coloured), so light scattered out of orange flesh stays orange.
- The white pith, the membrane star and the core read crisply on cut faces.
- Back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel studio reflections, GGX highlights, sugar-crystal glints.
- Post: Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither.

UI (editorial "Material Studies / No. 032", English)
- Italic serif title "Whole / Orange." with the caption "Eleven segments, set in jelly. Zest, pith and juice. Cut it as small as you like."
- Status pill "WEBGPU · LIVE".
- Tools: Hand / Knife. Varieties: Navel, Blood, Cara Cara.
- Firmness and Internal damping sliders; Give it a nudge, Reset, Pause; ¼ speed and Show mesh.
- Readouts: Mass (g, 1 unit ≈ 3 cm at 1.3 g/cm³), Volume (% of rest), Kinetic (mJ), Pieces.
- A collapsible "Inside the experiment" with notes on the method.
- Fallback without WebGPU. Stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.

prompt:

A 24 second square product launch video, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take that loops. The whole video happens inside the period of the wordmark. Nothing cuts: every scene grows out of the last, shapes morph, dots fly, colours change under floods. Every morph glides 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve. Banned: flat or gradient backgrounds made in code, camera zooms into tiny points, hard cuts, crossfades between scenes, bouncy springs, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, cropped type.

<structure>
Beats are the song's. The song enters on its big hit as the first pill appears.
Open: the letters slide into the period and vanish into it while it glides to the middle. The period opens like an iris onto the night inside it, and "you log off at 6", then "[product] doesn't", roll through one mask line over the night photo.
Ask: a glass "Ask [product]" pill springs in. The cursor clicks it, it glides into an input and the job types out.
Find: send shrinks the input to a dot that ripples into a 23x15 grid. A scan line sweeps it, 200 dots light up and a counter counts them.
Write: the lit dots pour into a glass email composer. A second, purple cursor labelled "[product]" types a personal opener and presses Send, and the counter runs to 200/200.
Night: the composer becomes a glass orb with a progress ring. A clock chip swaps 11:42 PM, 3:17 AM, 5:02 AM, 6:59 AM while the sky relights from night to dawn and "while you sleep" rolls in.
Results (beat 20): the orb turns black and goo-splits into the three result pills. The checks pop green.
Morning: the pills merge into a Dynamic Island that grows into a phone lock screen: the day photo, the date, a big 7:00, the bezel growing out of the screen edge. Three glass notifications stack in, and the cursor taps the first, which opens like iOS.
Proof: a week calendar (10 meetings pop in, a hover shows one's time), then a pipeline chart ($48,200 counts up, the line draws, a hover follows it). A black flood from the line's end becomes "Start your night shift →" and the cursor clicks it.
Out: the button shrinks into a dot, the whole scene closes down into it like an iris, and the letters slide back out of the period. The tagline rises. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Everything is a pure function of time inside seek(t): no timers, no state between frames.
2. One element morphs through every state (size, radius, colour, material) from a table of beat times, so retiming is one edit.

4. Glass: a pre-blurred copy of the photo clipped to the shape, then a tint and a gradient rim.
5. Goo: blur + alpha threshold on an offscreen layer for the split and the merge.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event, each placed by its measured peak. The song enters on its hit. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 4 motion-blur subframes. Scan every frame for single-frame jumps and fix each one.

A camera zoom into an off-centre dot swings sideways and spikes, so open the dot instead. Ease a closing iris by area, not radius, or its first frames jump. A helper that sets globalAlpha must restore the caller's, or fading cards pop. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's, or the digits smear.

title: Plush spider physics comparison

prompt:
Build "Plush Spider" — Material Studies No. 015.

Format and style:
- A single self-contained HTML file on native WebGPU, fully procedural (no assets, no libraries).

The specimen: a cute plush spider sitting on a table.
- The body is one signed distance field:
- a big round abdomen with knitted-looking stripes;
- a smaller head-and-chest tucked into it, with two fuzzy cheeks;

- The face:

- a row of four tiny bead eyes above them;

Physics — body:
- XPBD soft body on a hex-cell lattice: co-rotational shape matching plus tetrahedral volume, 60 Hz, 6 substeps.
- Gravity and floor friction. The seat keeps its footing.
- The toy slowly rights itself toward the heading it last walked (posture with a yaw).
- The abdomen breathes: its cells' rest shapes and rest volumes swell.

Physics — legs:
- Each leg is an XPBD rod chain from a hip embedded in the body lattice to the toe.
- A blended pose in the body's frame (sit, stand, hang, curl, wave) pulls each point toward its target: firmly at the hip, less toward the toe. So the legs hold their shape but sag and swing.
- The wire is plastic: when the hand bends a leg past its give, the pose itself takes the new shape and the leg stays bent until "Straighten legs".
- Spheres riding the body keep the legs off it. Toes grip the table. The finger pushes the legs aside.
- Pulling a leg further than it reaches tows the spider by that hip.

Behaviour:
- Walking:
- the body rises onto its legs with a height controller;
- it is led toward a goal with a weak pull and turns to face it;
- toes are drawn to footholds on the table;
- an alternating four-and-four gait lifts the set that has fallen furthest behind and sets it down ahead, with a little arc;
- it wanders on its own now and then.
- Curl up (button or a finger poke): the legs hug up over its back, the spider rolls away from the touch as a ball (no footing, no rolling resistance), then unrolls and rights itself.
- Hang on silk:
- a springy thread that only pulls, from an anchor high above to a patch of the back;
- it is reeled up off the table, swings when pushed, and its legs paddle the air;
- pressing again lowers it back to the table.
- Wave: one front leg is raised and wiggles.
- With the Finger tool, the spider scuttles over to the finger.

Rendering:
- Shell fur: base plus N instanced shells, alpha-to-coverage under 4× MSAA.
- The fur lie is carried by the deformation gradient, with a damped-spring tip lag.
- Kajiya–Kay highlights, velvet sheen, a comb tool.
- Regions painted in rest space: abdomen stripes, pale underside, short pile around the felt eye discs, cheeks, smile groove, stitched seams round the hips.
- Legs are drawn each frame as plush tubes:
- swept along a Catmull–Rom curve through each rod with a parallel-transport frame;
- a slight knee bulge and a rounded little foot;
- banded colour and a shorter pile.
- A thin glinting silk thread.
- Soft PCSS key-light shadows, contact occlusion on the studio floor, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping.
- NaN-safe WGSL: clamped pow and smoothstep, clamped post.

UI:

- Finger: the spider follows it, and a poke curls it up;
- Comb: brush the pile.

title: Code-generated pixel art life story film
author: twoclipping
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a voiceover or song with a spoken line (the audio file) and its transcript, 10-12 small objects that sum up my life, two silhouettes to light like a heat camera (a head in profile and a raised hand), and the 3 words I want to land hardest. If I skip any, use the defaults: vinyl, book, camera, cat, coin, game controller, cap, heart, money, plant, clapperboard, skateboard; free CC0 silhouettes from Openverse; action, intention, curiosity.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 20 second 4:3 film, 1440x1080 at 60fps, cut to the voice. Off-white paper, black, one red, one yellow, Geist for every word. Film grain on everything, a soft vignette, and a camera that never rests: a slow handheld float under everything plus a slow push inside every scene.
No scene cuts to the next: each handoff starts on the exact last frame of the scene before. The only hard cuts are the beat flips on the last word.
Every object is pixel art you draw yourself: a 16x16 grid per object, every cell a hand-placed colour, rendered as a 3D block (a darker extrusion down-right, a thin bevel on every cell) with a soft contact shadow.
The silhouettes are lit like a heat camera: the heat comes from how thick the body is at each point, so the nose, the hair and the fingertips run cooler, plus one hotspot and a slow moving noise, mapped through a black > red > orange > cream ramp. The edge stays razor sharp, with a soft glow outside it.
Motion rules: nothing pops in (eased glides of about 0.5s with a soft start), fast moves get real motion blur instead of ghost copies, and captions type with the voice behind a block cursor.
Banned: stock footage, AI video, 3D camera moves, particles, glitch.
</direction>

<structure>
Hang every scene on the transcript's word timings (measure them with faster-whisper word timestamps, one short chunk at a time):
1. The first word fills a yellow card. The card wipes off to the left and the question types underneath on two centred lines that glide to stay centred as they grow, the key word underlined in red as it's spoken.
2. The objects streak past in lanes above and below the words, a cyan four-point flare sweeps in, then the page burns away: black closes in from the edges onto the head, behind a hot red edge.
3. The head heats up on black while the answer types low on the left. A thin white orbit draws itself around the head, its far half passing behind it. On the last word, paper blooms out from inside the head with the objects in it, and the camera falls through: the head rushes past the lens until the paper is all we see.
4. The objects sit on a tilted ring seen in perspective (the front ones bigger and lower, drawn last), slowly turning, each one bobbing; the coin flips and lands with sparks.
5. On each of the 3 words, that object flies out of the ring to the left and grows, the page floods black from it, and the word types beside it (camera: a red shutter star; book: a red ribbon sweep; record: two white orbits and red notes). Then the flood drains back into the object as it flies home, and the camera dives closer into the ring. Put each hero object in the slot that is front-left when its word lands.
6. The ring pulls in a touch, bursts outward, every object turns to ink, and ink blots grow and swallow the page.
7. The hand rises into frame, hot, with the line split either side of it. The heart drops into its palm, then lifts to the centre at the size the next scene holds it.
8. The last word, one letter per beat, the background flipping paper / black / red, the heart holding its place across the cut, the centre object morphing pixel by pixel into the next one.
9. Thin brush strokes sweep through, the letters drift apart and float, then settle back into the word with the heart above it. The camera keeps pushing through the hold.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. Bake each pixel sprite once to an offscreen canvas (the extrusion layers, then the face), then draw it scaled and rotated.
3. The heat: precompute each silhouette's base heat once (a distance transform of the mask, held at the edge value outside it so nothing dark bleeds in when it is upscaled). Every frame, add the hotspot and two octaves of value noise at quarter resolution, map it through a 256-step lookup, upscale it, and cut it with the full-resolution mask.
4. The fall through the head: draw the ring scene into an offscreen layer, mask it with the head scaled up about a point inside the skull, and grow that scale on a cubed curve until the head covers the frame. The ring inside zooms less than the head does, so it reads as depth.
5. The pixel morph: pair every cell of object A with a cell of object B and glide each one's position and colour, with a small random delay per cell.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes, then lay the original audio back on with ffmpeg.
</build>

<gotchas>
A mask PNG with no alpha channel fills the whole box with heat, so put the silhouette in the alpha. A limb cut by the photo's border shows as a straight edge, so extend the mask past the frame. A handoff only reads as smooth when the last frame of one scene is the first frame of the next: draw the outgoing scene under the transition, and give scenes that show the same ring one shared zoom function. A flood that's still retreating when the next scene starts reads as a hard cut, so let it finish first. A fast ease-out flood reads as a jump; use a soft start.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, measure the word timings, then show me 8 stills before you render.
</start>

title: Arctic jelly iceberg diorama comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Iceberg Jelly" — the next piece in my "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas: a single self-contained HTML file using WebGPU (WGSL), no external libraries, English UI.

THE SCENE
A square block of jelly (5.2 × 5.2 units) standing on a pale, cool-grey paper studio backdrop with a soft floor shadow. Inside it, a polar bay:
- At the back left, a glacier flows down a valley between jagged mountains and ends in an ice cliff standing in deep water. The cliff has vertical runnels and blue bands. The glacier surface has chevron crevasses along its margins, transverse crevasses and seracs near the front, and grey lateral moraines. Its tongue is flanked by moraine banks, so only its front stands in the water.
- Mountains: a peaky left range and a spur on the right of the glacier, with a snowy ridge along the back. Dark volcanic rock with orange lichen, and snow in ragged patches on flatter and higher ground (not everywhere).
- At the back right, a low peninsula with an Adélie penguin rookery: an organic, irregular patch of round pebbles stained pink with krill, with pebble-ring nests. Behind it, a small research station (red and yellow huts on stilts, fuel drums, a radio mast with guy wires, a flag, a turning anemometer, a snowmobile) and a timber quay.
- A ragged skerry of two low rocks off to the front right, where Weddell seals haul out.
- The sea floor is grey gravel with shells, sponges, sea stars and swaying anemones, visible through the clear jelly front face.
- The cut faces of the block show candy-coloured strata, dark basalt columns under the land, and layered blue glacier ice with a dirty basal layer under the glacier.

PHYSICS
- Shallow-water simulation on a ~168² grid for the bay: waves, wakes, foam, refraction, caustics on the floor, light shafts, and absorption that depends on the flavour.
- Every piece of ice is a rigid body: tabular, dome, pinnacle and wedge bergs, growlers, pancake floes, and glacier slabs. Each is a star-shaped faceted mesh (superellipsoid plus lobes plus two octaves of noise), a lattice of mass points for buoyancy and drag, and contact spheres for ground, walls, each other and the ship. Settle stable poses at load so nothing capsizes at the start.
- Calving: three slabs stand along the cliff. About once a minute (or on demand) one breaks off with a crack, a puff of ice dust, a splash, spray and a wave, then capsizes until it finds a stable way up. The glacier slowly pushes a new slab out. Old slabs melt away.
- The displaced water is handed back to the waves without feedback: wakes only when a piece moves fast, splashes when it plunges in. Slow drift makes no waves.
- The jelly block itself wobbles, shears and squashes, and can be tipped by dragging its side.

title: Harbor jelly water physics comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Harbor Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (no external requests, no libraries) that renders an interactive 3D diorama with WebGPU/WGSL: a small working container harbor set inside a square block of wobbly, translucent jelly sea, sitting on a paper studio backdrop. It belongs to a series called "Material Studies", so match that look: warm paper background, serif italic display title ("Harbor Jelly."), small uppercase eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a status pill top-right ("WebGPU · Live"), a frosted control panel on the right, and a "How to play" line bottom-left. English UI. Light theme only, by design.

THE BLOCK
- A 5.2 × 5.2 block seen from a 3/4 orbit camera. The ground and sea are cut flat at the block's sides, so you see candy-coloured soil strata in cross-section, and the sea's cut faces show everything underwater through the jelly.
- The water is a real-time linear shallow-water simulation on a staggered grid (heights at cell centres, velocities on faces) with a little surface tension, so it feels like jelly. Render it with refraction, absorption by depth, caustics projected onto the floor, light shafts, a Fresnel studio reflection, foam (wakes, splashes, a shoreline lace) and a bright meniscus on the cut edges.
- The whole block can be tipped by dragging its side. The water sloshes to the low side, the jelly shears and quivers, then it settles flat again.

THE HARBOR (layout)
- Along the back runs a vertical concrete quay wall, with rubber fenders, bollards, ladders, and mussels and weed crusting it below the waterline.
- Left part: a container terminal. A flat asphalt yard with painted lines, concrete strips with two crane rails, light towers, and a small terminal office. Hundreds of colourful containers are stacked in neat rows. Each is a ribbed steel box with door ends and darker corner posts, drawn as GPU instances in about ten liveries.
- Right part: an old stone fishing quay with a cobbled promenade, a corrugated fish-market shed and lamp posts. A timber pier stands on mussel-covered piles with cross-bracing, with two small fishing boats moored alongside.
- Behind it all, a town climbs a grassy hill: three rows of gabled houses in Nordic harbour colours (falu red, ochre, white, pale blue, mint, pink) with tiled or slate roofs, white-framed windows, doors and chimneys. There is a white church with a green copper spire, and some round trees.
- A rubble breakwater shelters the fishing harbour, with a concrete crown wall. Big rocks sit near the crest, smaller weedy ones tumble down under water. On its head stands a red-and-white banded lighthouse with a gallery and a glass lantern, whose lamp slowly turns.
- In the open basin: two small yachts swinging on their moorings (white hulls, coloured stripe, fin keels visible through the jelly, furled sails), yellow mooring buoys, and a green channel buoy, all bobbing on the waves.
- On the floor: pale sand with drifts of silt, weed tufts, stones, starfish, an old anchor with chain, a lost tyre.

THE SHIP'S DAY (fully automatic loop, about 100 s)
1. A small feeder container ship (navy topsides, red antifouling, white accommodation block at the stern with bridge wings, funnel with a yellow band, turning radar, visible propeller) lies alongside with containers on deck, 6 bays × 4 rows × 2 tiers.
2. Two ship-to-shore gantry cranes on the rails, one red and one blue, each with portal legs, a backreach with a machinery house, an A-frame with forestays, a hinged boom, a trolley with a hanging cab, and a yellow spreader on four wire falls. They lower their booms and swap boxes: unload from the tops of the ship's stacks into yard stacks, then load other boxes aboard. Every move is a smooth sequence: travel, trolley out, lower onto the box (tracking the ship's bobbing), latch, hoist, trolley across, lower, unlatch. Cranes never get closer than their leg width; an idle crane moves out of the other's way.
3. When the work is done the trolleys park, the booms swing up, and a tug comes round to the bow. The tug has a black hull, white and red superstructure, a tyre fender all round, a big bow fender, and puffs of funnel smoke. It passes a tow line and backs away, pulling the bow off the quay while the ship swings out. Then the line is cast off, the tug pivots on the spot and goes home, and the ship sounds her horn.
4. The ship sails a lap of the harbour along a smooth path, past the lighthouse. She rides the water on several sample points (heave, pitch, roll) and hands the displaced water back to the sim, so she leaves a real bow wave, wake and white water.
5. Meanwhile the tug goes out to a standby spot. When the ship stops off the quay, the tug noses in and pushes her sideways onto the fenders, with prop wash churning. Then it backs off, the booms come down, and the cranes start again.
- Keep everything collision-free (ship and tug vs. quay, breakwater, pier, yachts and buoy; no grounding). Check it with a headless node test.

LIFE
- Fish schools (mackerel, herring, small orange wrasse) as boids that stay in the water and under the hulls, scatter from fingers, splashes and moving ships, and come to food.
- Moon jellyfish: glassy pulsing bells with four pink rings, frilly oral arms and a fringe of tentacles. They drift with the water flow.
- Herring gulls (white body, grey mantle, black wingtips, yellow bill with a red spot). They circle, bank and glide, and land on perches: lamps, roof ridges, the church spire, the lighthouse gallery, the crane apexes, the ship's mast, the tug, the yachts' masthead. Perches on moving things move with them. They all take off when the horn sounds, and some dive at food.
- Steam puffs from the ship's funnel on the horn; tiny bubbles caught in the jelly.

CONTROLS (right panel; bottom sheet on phones)
- "Cast off" sends the ship early (cranes finish the box in hand). At sea the button becomes "Call her in" and hurries her home; it greys out while busy.
- "Horn" (also Space) plays a synthesized WebAudio ship horn: two low detuned sawtooth reeds a fifth apart, low-passed, starting only after a user gesture. It also blows steam and scatters the gulls.
- "Feed the fish" scatters pellets off the end of the pier; fish rush in and gulls swoop down.
- Tally: Boxes moved / Voyages / Fed. A ship status line ("Unloading 3 / 8", "Loading", "Booms up", "Tug coming", "Casting off", "At sea 40%", "Coming in", "Berthing"). A small activity meter.
- Flavour swatches change the water colour and strata: Sea glass (teal-mint), Blueberry (deep blue), Lime.
- Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Tide (±10 cm; the sea level, ships and floating things follow).
- Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, Reset view.

POINTER INTERACTION
- Drag across the water to make waves (with a crosshair cursor).
- Drag the side of the block to tip it.
- Pick up an orange-and-white lifebuoy and throw it. Lifebuoys float flat on the waves, bounce off the pier, buildings and breakwater, and are shoved aside by the ship and tug.
- Drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.
- On phones: touch orbit, pinch zoom, and a collapsible bottom sheet for the controls.

RENDERING DETAILS
- Pipeline: shadow map → caustics pass → opaque scene (with a distance buffer) → back-face pass of the water → water pass over a copy of the scene → tone map + dither.
- Moving rigs are static vertex buffers whose vertices carry an object id; about 24 object transforms (position + quaternion) live in the uniform buffer. Cables are drawn with one end in each object's frame, so they stretch: crane falls, forestays, the tow line.
- Material kinds in the prop shader: matte paint, glass, gloss steel, roof tiles, timber grain, corrugated sheet (normal-perturbed ribs), dressed-stone masonry, rubber, rock, glowing lamps, swaying weed, and hulls with antifouling below a boot-top line.
- The jelly shear and squash wobble applies to everything inside the block.

QUALITY BAR
- Smooth on a laptop; simulation under about 2 ms per frame.
- A friendly fallback screen if WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails.
- No console errors, no page scroll. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
- Ship it with a headless test of the choreography and a Playwright end-to-end test.

title: Code-generated music video
author: kloss_xyz
prompt:
You're a motion director and creative coder. Make a finished music video for [song file], built entirely in code and rendered frame by frame.

Concept: [your idea in one or two sentences]
Look: [palette, mood, references]
On-screen text: [title only / none / lyrics]
Deliver: [full song or mm:ss to mm:ss], [16:9 / 9:16 / both, each recomposed, not cropped], [fps], H.264 + AAC for [platform]

How to work:
1. Analyze the song before any visuals. Split it into bands or stems and export per-frame features plus a timing map (beats, bars, sections, hits). Every visual event reads from the map and is listed in it.
2. Give each musical element one visual job that serves the concept. Keep one idea transforming across the song instead of cycling effects.
3. Storyboard with timings and 3 style frames, get a fresh critic's verdict on them, then a 4-second end-to-end test before the full build.
4. Make every value a pure function of the frame number. Render offline, encode with the original audio (gain only).
5. After each full render, send it to fresh critic subagents that never saw the build, each returning ranked problems with timestamps and a ship / one more pass verdict:
- sound-off: retells the story from a silent 2 fps contact sheet
- sync: every cut, hit and visual event within 1 frame of the timing map
- QA: specs, palette, text, artifacts, measured on the frames
- director: brutal critique against the brief
- one per extra aspect ratio: composition and platform UI zones
6. Fix render bugs first, then the biggest problem; re-render; log each round with before/after numbers. If critics conflict, the brief wins.
7. Stop after [5] rounds or when the bar passes. The final pass checks only for breakage.

The bar: exact duration, size and fps; frame one finished; no still over 0.5 s; cuts and hits within 1 frame; audio unedited except gain, about -14 LUFS, true peak under -1 dB; text readable and inside safe areas; understood with the sound off.

author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive low-poly 3D diorama of a rural Japanese railway station in spring, using Three.js (ES modules from a CDN). No external models or images — generate all geometry from primitives in code and paint textures (grass, signs) on <canvas>.

Style: a floating diorama block (grass top, layered earth and stone sides) on a soft pastel sky gradient. MeshToonMaterial with a 3-step gradient map, dark ink outlines (OutlineEffect), soft directional shadows, bright saturated palette.

Scene:
- A single railway track across the block, running into green tunnel hills with concrete portals at both ends.
- Concrete platform with a yellow tactile strip, a shelter with a corrugated roof, benches, a hanging clock, a small station building with a teal gable roof and a "春風駅" sign, a station name board (はるかぜ / Harukaze, with neighbouring stations), vending machines, bins, lamps, fence.
- A road crossing the track with a level crossing: striped poles, crossbuck, red flashing lamps, barrier arms; road markings and "止まれ".
- Utility poles with sagging wires, overhead catenary, small village houses, a vegetable patch, bushes, and cherry trees with puffy pink blob crowns and fallen petals painted on the grass.

Animation:
- A two-car commuter train (white with a pink stripe, pantograph) comes out of one tunnel, stops at the platform, then departs into the other; clipping planes hide it inside the tunnels. Loop every ~32 s.
- Crossing lamps blink alternately and the arms lower before the train passes, then rise.
- ~460 instanced sakura petals drifting in the wind.
- Slow auto-orbit camera; OrbitControls for drag and zoom.

UI (English): bottom-left title "春風駅 / Harukaze Station" with a small caption; bottom-right glass toolbar with Day / Night, Orbit on/off, and Train (call the next train). Night mode: dark sky with stars, lit windows, lamp point lights with additive glow sprites, glowing crossing lamps and train headlights.

Technical: merge static meshes by material into a few dozen draw calls; use a seeded random so the scene is identical on every load; responsive down to phone width; respect prefers-reduced-motion.

title: Interactive plush penguin model comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Penguin": editorial studio layout, large italic serif title "Plush / Penguin.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 016", caption "A fluffy egg on two felt feet. It waddles, it toboggans, it falls over — and always gets back up.", live status chip, specimen panel on the right, stats row (Mass, Volume, Steps, Slide in cm), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. UI in English, works on mobile.

The toy: a round plush penguin chick — an egg-shaped stuffed body as one SDF meshed with surface nets, a dark cap and back, a pale fluffy face and belly, big glossy safety-glass eyes, a small felt beak, pink cheeks, two flat felt feet. Its flippers are separate cloth pieces (particle cloth sewn to points embedded in the body) that flop, flap and stretch.

Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, live volume readout), skinned to the mesh, standing on a table with Coulomb friction. Locomotion by posture: a weak pull of the whole body toward its rest shape turned to an orientation and carried with its centre of mass, so the stuffing does the moving. Behaviours: Waddle (rocks side to side, lifting each foot and setting it down ahead), Belly slide (a little hop, flops forward onto its tummy and toboggans across the table, then rocks back up), Flap (happy flapping and a couple of hops), Topple (falls onto its back, belly or side and rocks itself upright with an overshoot), Smooth fur, Reset. Finger: it waddles over to your finger; push it and it falls over. Hand: pick it up, squash it, pull a flipper and it comes along.

Fur: real-time shell fur with alpha-to-coverage — long fluffy down on the body, short on the face, combable with a Comb tool (against the grain darker, with it shinier). Sliders: Stuffing, Pile (mm), Table (felt ↔ ice friction, so it slides further on ice). Palettes: Chick, Classic, Little blue. ¼ speed and mesh toggles, Pause. 60 fps.
